title: The Vegan Sausage Roll
hook: A sausage roll launched like a new phone.
before: Greggs was a high-street bakery best known for its pork sausage roll, not for following food trends.
idea: On 3 January 2019, during Veganuary, Greggs launched a vegan sausage roll with a film that borrowed the style of a tech launch.
shift: Piers Morgan complained on Twitter, Greggs replied with a joke, and the launch became national news. It was the company’s fastest-selling launch in more than six years.
measure: Like-for-like sales growth in the seven weeks to 16 February 2019, from Greggs’ trading update. Total sales rose 14.1%
evidence: Greggs credited the vegan sausage roll for strong trading and raised its profit outlook. That is a business trend: the new product, the publicity and the wider range all moved together.
lesson: A product can be the ad, if it says something about the brand nobody expected.
test: The company’s trading update reported sales in the weeks after launch.
links: Read the profit update · ITV News
memorable: It treated a £1 pastry with the reverence of a gadget, and that joke did half the work.

creative.label: Watch ‘The Greggs Vegan Sausage Roll’ on Greggs’ channel

impact_source: Read the trading report · City A.M.
metric_label: Like-for-like sales, seven weeks after launch
take: The best launch of the decade, and it was a sausage roll. The product changed the brand more than any campaign could have.

image.credit: Greggs, The Vegan Sausage Roll (2019) · launch film still

title: The Three-Point Seatbelt
hook: Volvo invented the modern seatbelt, then let every rival use it.
before: Car seatbelts in the 1950s were mostly lap belts, and many cars had none.
idea: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin designed the three-point belt, and Volvo fitted it in 1959. The company left the patent open so any carmaker could use the design for free.
shift: Safety became the thing Volvo stood for, decades before it was a selling point for anyone else.
measure: Volvo’s estimate of lives saved. Other estimates are lower, so treat it as an order of magnitude
evidence: The invention and the open patent are well recorded. The lives-saved figure is Volvo’s own estimate, and no public source measures what the decision did for Volvo’s sales.
lesson: The strongest brand promise is one the product keeps for you.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the invention, the patent decision and Volvo’s estimate of its effect.
links: Watch ‘Volvo’s three-point safety belt’ on the SafestCar channel
memorable: It is a brand built on a gift to its competitors.

creative.label: Watch Volvo’s archive film on the development of the three-point seatbelt, 1959 to 1999
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the company’s account · Volvo Group
take: Every safety ad Volvo has made since is an echo of this one decision. The product was the campaign before anyone wrote a line.

image.alt: Nils Bohlin in the driver’s seat demonstrating Volvo’s three-point seatbelt
image.credit: Nils Bohlin with the three-point belt · Volvo Group heritage archive

title: Walkman
hook: A tape player with no speaker, and a new way to live with music.
before: Music came from radios, record players and car stereos. Listening was something you did in a room, or shared.
idea: In July 1979 Sony launched the Walkman TPS-L2, a small cassette player with lightweight headphones.
shift: Sales started slowly, then the first 30,000 sold out within about two months. Sony became the name for personal music for a generation.
measure: Units of every Walkman format sold by March 2009, as widely reported. About 200m were cassette players
evidence: The sales are widely reported. They show the product’s success, not the effect of any single campaign.
lesson: If a product changes a habit, the brand becomes the name of the habit.
test: The record is unit sales over thirty years.
links: Hear from the engineers behind the original Walkman · Sony
memorable: Headphones in public, which looked odd in 1979 and normal ever since.

creative.label: Watch the 1979 Walkman advert in Smithsonian Music’s archive
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Walkman players of every type, 1979 to 2009
take: Sony’s engineers made a product the sales team doubted, and it defined the brand for twenty years. That’s still the best argument for listening to product people.

image.alt: Two performers in headphones hold up a blue Sony Walkman
image.credit: Sony Walkman TV advert (1979) · still from the upload catalogued by Smithsonian Music

title: From Sickbed to Stadium
hook: A drink for sick children became a drink for athletes.
before: Lucozade was sold as a drink for people recovering from illness, wrapped in yellow cellophane and kept for the sickroom.
idea: Beecham repositioned it as an energy drink. ‘Aids recovery’ became ‘replaces lost energy’, and Olympic decathlete Daley Thompson fronted the campaign from 1983.
shift: The same drink was seen as a fitness product by younger people, and the brand grew far beyond the sickroom.
measure: Growth in volume sales reported in the IPA paper, after the first campaign was found not to work
evidence: The IPA paper reports a 40% increase in volume sales and better image among the target group. Other sources say UK sales tripled to almost £75m between 1984 and 1989. Both are trends.
lesson: Sometimes the product is right and the story around it is the problem.
test: Tracking showed why the first Daley Thompson campaign didn’t work. Volume sales were measured after the revised campaign.
links: Explore the archived Daley Thompson training campaign · History of Advertising Trust
memorable: It kept the drink and changed the patient into an athlete.

creative.label: Watch Daley Thompson in the Ogilvy Museum’s Lucozade advert
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Volume sales after the revised campaign
take: I love that the IPA paper admits the first campaign failed. The product didn’t change, the reason to drink it did.
data_source: A recovery drink became an energy drink

image.alt: Daley Thompson sprinting in a white vest in the Lucozade Energy advert
image.credit: Lucozade, Daley Thompson advert · still from the Ogilvy Museum archive

title: The Plastic Swiss Watch
hook: Switzerland answered cheap quartz watches with a cheaper, better one.
before: Cheap quartz watches, mainly from Japan, had pushed the Swiss industry into crisis. Hundreds of watchmakers had gone.
idea: In 1983 the two largest Swiss watch groups merged and launched the Swatch, a plastic quartz watch made with far fewer parts than usual.
shift: A Swiss watch became a cheap, collectable fashion item, and the group behind it later took the Swatch name.
measure: The number of parts in the movement. A production fact, not a result
evidence: Swatch is widely credited with helping rescue Swiss watchmaking, though some historians give more credit to the luxury brands that followed. No public source isolates the brand effect.
lesson: When you can’t win on price, make the cheap version the desirable one.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the industry’s recovery and the company’s history.
memorable: It made a watch something you changed with your outfit.
metric_label: Parts in a Swatch, down from about 100
take: Cheap and Swiss sounded like a contradiction. Swatch turned it into the point.
data_source: A cheap watch for an expensive industry

image.alt: Early Swatch print advert showing a watch amid blue waves
image.credit: Swatch, early print advertising · Swatch Group archive

title: Draught in a Can
medium: Product launch, TV, posters and press
hook: Pub Guinness at home. Hard to believe, so they had to prove it.
before: Drinkers believed proper draught Guinness only existed in the pub, poured from a tap.
idea: Guinness launched draught in cans with a widget that recreated the creamy head. Ogilvy’s launch campaign tackled the disbelief directly, starting in three test regions.
shift: The pub pint came home, and the brand reached people who didn’t drink draught Guinness.
measure: Share of trial among people new to Draught Guinness, per the IPA paper. Half went on to try it in pubs
evidence: The IPA paper reports sales success for the cans and for Guinness as a whole, with fast increases in awareness and trial. It is a sales and trial trend from a test-market launch.
lesson: When the product sounds too good to be true, the ad’s job is to make it believable.
test: A test market in three regions measured awareness, trial and sales before the national launch.
links: Licence for the widget photograph · CC BY-SA 4.0
memorable: A small plastic ball in a can, and a nation listening for the hiss.

creative.label: Watch BigClive cut open a Guinness Draught can and examine the floating widget
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Of people trying it were new to Draught Guinness
take: The widget is the hero, but the brief is the clever bit. Ogilvy sold the proof, not the beer.
data_source: A widget that made pub Guinness at home

title: DC01
hook: A vacuum cleaner that let you watch it work.
before: Vacuum cleaners used bags that clogged and lost suction. Hoover and others led the UK market.
idea: After thousands of prototypes, James Dyson launched the bagless DC01 in 1993 at around twice the price of rivals, with a clear bin so you could see what it picked up.
shift: The product was its own demonstration. It became Britain’s best-selling vacuum cleaner within about two years.
measure: The time to the top of the UK market, per Wikipedia. Other sources say about two years
evidence: Market share figures from the time put Dyson ahead of Hoover within about two years. That is a sales trend for a product sold with little advertising.
lesson: If people can see the product work, you don’t need to tell them it does.
test: The record is market share and sales rank.
memorable: The clear bin. Watching dust spin is strangely satisfying, and it sold the machine.

creative.label: Watch James Dyson revisit the DC01 in Invention: A Life
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: To become the UK’s best-selling vacuum
take: The clear bin is the best piece of advertising Dyson ever made, and it’s a design decision.
data_source: A see-through bin that showed the dirt

image.credit: Dyson DC01 · Centre Pompidou, MNAM-CCI / Bertrand Prévost / Dist. GrandPalaisRmn

title: Prius
hook: A car that made fuel economy something to show off.
before: Hybrid cars were concepts and experiments. Fuel economy was something people wanted, not something they displayed.
idea: Toyota launched the Prius in Japan in December 1997 as the first mass-produced hybrid, then took it to other markets from 2000.
shift: The Prius became the shorthand for green motoring, and Toyota became the hybrid brand.
measure: Cumulative worldwide sales announced by Toyota in May 2008
evidence: Toyota’s own milestones show the growth in sales. They show the product’s success, not what any campaign added.
lesson: Be first in a new category, and you can own its name for years.
test: The record is Toyota’s announced sales milestones.
memorable: Its odd shape. It looked different on purpose, so everyone knew what you drove.

creative.label: Watch the original Japanese Prius commercial
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The shape did the marketing. A hybrid that looked like any other car would never have become a badge.

title: It’s a Skoda. Honest
hook: The car was good. The jokes were the problem.
before: Skoda jokes were part of British culture. VW had bought the brand in 1991 and improved the cars, but nobody noticed.
idea: For the Fabia launch in March 2000, Fallon London faced the prejudice head on, with ads in which people couldn’t believe a car this good was a Skoda.
shift: Making fun of the joke disarmed it. People looked at the cars again.
measure: UK sales growth reported in the IPA paper, well ahead of other markets with the same model mix
evidence: The IPA paper reports that people rejecting the brand fell from 60% to 42%, and UK sales grew 64%, much faster than in other markets. The comparison with other markets strengthens the case, but it is still a trend.
lesson: When the product has changed and opinion hasn’t, name the opinion.
test: Brand tracking measured rejection of the marque, and sales were compared with other markets selling the same cars.
memorable: It is a brand laughing at itself, which is very British and very disarming.

creative.label: Watch Factory Tour, a 2000 Škoda Fabia television advert
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The product had already been fixed. The campaign just gave people permission to notice. Edition 01’s ‘Think Small’ would approve.

data_source: A better car nobody believed in

title: The New MINI
hook: BMW brought back a British icon and made it premium.
before: The original Mini was loved but old. BMW, which had owned Rover, kept the MINI brand when it sold the rest.
idea: In 2001 BMW launched a new MINI, built at Oxford, that kept the look of the original and sold it as a premium small car.
shift: A small car became a fashion statement with a price to match. BMW said production quickly outran its plans.
measure: Cars built at Plant Oxford in the first fifteen years, per BMW
evidence: BMW’s figures show a long-running sales success. They show the product’s success, not what the launch campaigns added.
lesson: Heritage sells when the product delivers on it.
test: The record is BMW’s production figures.
links: Watch another UK launch advert from 2001
memorable: It looks like the old Mini at a glance and like nothing else up close.

creative.label: Watch Mini Martians from the UK launch campaign
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Edition 05 is full of brands that changed what people loved and paid for it. MINI changed almost everything and kept the bit people loved.
data_source: An icon rebuilt as a premium car

title: Wii
hook: Gaming for people who didn’t play games.
before: Consoles competed on graphics and power, built for people who already played.
idea: Nintendo’s Wii used a motion controller and simple games such as Wii Sports so anyone could pick it up.
shift: Grandparents bowled in living rooms. Nintendo widened who a gamer was.
measure: Lifetime unit sales in Nintendo’s published figures
evidence: Nintendo’s figures show huge sales. They show the product’s success, not what the advertising added.
lesson: Sometimes the biggest market is the people the category ignored.
test: The record is Nintendo’s published unit sales.
memorable: People waving their arms at the television, of every age.

creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the sales report · Game Informer
take: The Wii put people in the picture that the industry had left out. That’s Representation, done with a product instead of a cast.

title: iPhone
hook: A phone, an iPod and an internet device in one.
before: Phones had keypads and small screens. Apple sold computers and iPods.
idea: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone in January 2007, and it went on sale on 29 June.
shift: Apple became a phone company, and the phone became the centre of people’s digital lives.
measure: The time from launch to the millionth sale, per Apple. An analyst estimated fewer sales by the end of July
evidence: Apple’s own announcement gives the milestone. It is self-reported, and it shows demand for the product rather than the effect of the advertising.
lesson: The best launch shows people something they didn’t know they wanted.
test: The record is Apple’s announced sales milestone.
links: Licence for the Macworld photograph · CC BY 2.0
memorable: The keynote itself. Jobs repeated ‘an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator’ until the audience realised it was one device.

creative.label: Watch Steve Jobs introduce the iPhone at Macworld in 2007
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Edition 01 had Apple’s ‘1984’. This is the product that finally lived up to it.
data_source: A phone with one screen and no keypad

title: Vaporfly and Breaking2
hook: A shoe so fast the sport changed its rules.
before: Shoes were sold on comfort and style. Nobody claimed a shoe could make you measurably faster.
idea: In May 2017 Nike ran Breaking2, an attempt to break two hours for the marathon at Monza, with athletes in its new carbon-plated shoe.
shift: Eliud Kipchoge ran 2:00:25. The Vaporfly became the shoe every serious runner wanted, and in 2020 World Athletics tightened its rules on shoes.
measure: The time Kipchoge ran at Monza. A creative fact, not a result
evidence: A New York Times analysis of race data found Vaporfly runners were faster than similar runners in other shoes. That is evidence about the shoe. No public source shows the effect on Nike’s sales.
lesson: If your product is the best, let the stopwatch say so.
test: The record is race times, independent analysis of race data and the rule change.
links: Watch WIRED explain the science behind Breaking2
memorable: A world-class athlete running laps of a motor-racing circuit at dawn, behind a car.

creative.label: Watch the Breaking2 documentary on filmmaker Brett Nicoletti’s Vimeo
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Most brands would kill for proof like a rule change. Nike made the product so good the governing body had to answer it.
data_source: A shoe tested on the world’s best

image.alt: Eliud Kipchoge, Zersenay Tadese and Lelisa Desisa in Nike’s Breaking2 launch photography

title: The Adaptive Controller
hook: A controller designed with the players other controllers left out.
before: Standard controllers assumed two hands and fine motor control. Many gamers with limited mobility had to improvise.
idea: Microsoft designed the Xbox Adaptive Controller with gamers with disabilities and accessibility charities. It went on sale in 2018, in packaging that could be opened easily.
shift: Accessibility became part of what Xbox stands for, not a side project.
measure: The campaign won a Cannes Grand Prix, and the product won a D&AD Black Pencil, both in 2019. Awards, not results
evidence: The product won a D&AD Black Pencil and its campaign won a Cannes Grand Prix. No public source shows sales or brand effects.
lesson: Design for the people at the edges, and the whole brand looks different.
test: There is no published effectiveness record, only awards.
links: Read about the Grand Prix · Ad Age
memorable: Even the box was designed to open easily. The care shows everywhere.

creative.label: Watch ‘Introducing the Xbox Adaptive Controller’ on Xbox’s channel

impact_source: Read the award story · Microsoft UK
take: Purpose you can hold in your hands. After Edition 05’s borrowed causes, this is the opposite: a brand that built the thing first.
data_source: A controller for gamers with disabilities

image.alt: White Xbox Adaptive Controller connected to four coloured switches
image.credit: Xbox Adaptive Controller with external switches (2018) · Microsoft

title: Guinness 0.0
hook: The pint that lets non-drinkers stay in the round.
before: Alcohol-free beer was a compromise, and non-drinkers in the pub had little to order.
idea: Guinness launched an alcohol-free stout in Great Britain in 2020. Soon after launch it was recalled over a quality problem, then relaunched.
shift: Guinness 0.0 overtook Heineken 0.0 to become the UK’s biggest alcohol-free beer, while the Guinness brand reached more women and younger drinkers.
measure: Its ranking after overtaking Heineken 0.0, per The Grocer
evidence: Trade press reports Guinness 0.0 as the UK’s biggest alcohol-free beer, alongside strong growth for the Guinness brand. That is a sales trend, and the whole brand was growing at the same time.
lesson: A product can widen who a brand is for without changing what it stands for.
test: The record is market rankings and Diageo’s results.
links: Read how Guinness reached new drinkers · Marketing Week
Read the October 2020 launch announcement · Diageo
memorable: It looks exactly like a pint of Guinness, which is the whole point in a pub.

creative.label: Watch the singing pints in Holding Out for a ZERO, Guinness’s 2023 campaign
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the ranking report · The Grocer
metric_label: Alcohol-free beer in the UK, per The Grocer
take: It survived a recall in its first weeks, which would have finished most launches in Edition 05. The product was good enough to come back.
data_source: A pint for people who aren’t drinking
